title: Eleven Seconds
passages:
The drum brought them up the last four meters with the pony bottle flat on zero — the spare cylinder a diver clips at the hip, good for one bad minute — and Bayo dropped the brake pawl into the drum gear before the wire could run out under it. It bit with a sound like a jar of nails going downstairs. Then the deck was all hands. Sol got her arms under Wren's harness, Nia took the legs, and between them they folded her over the rail and down onto the mat beside Dey, in rain that came warm and straight and loud in the eye of the thing.

Salas came up in the sling with his lamp still off. Bayo unhooked him and he went straight to his hands and knees and brought up channel water, a lot of it, the way a bilge pump does.

"Pony's dry," Sol said. "Both sets."

"It was dry at thirty-one," Wren said. Her voice came out sanded down. She lay flat with the deck lights in her eyes and her left fist shut against her chest, and she knew what was in it only by the beacon ticking in her palm — one ping a second, a locator chirp so a crew can find a dropped can in the dark, and this one had been chirping up at them out of the tower since before the bell struck ten.

"Open your hand," Sol said.

"I can't tell you what's in it."

"Then open it and we'll both find out."

"I mean I can't tell you what I went down for." Wren turned her head. Dey was a foot away, gray as wet cement, the bag in Sol's other hand going in and out for him, and he watched her with the flat interest of a man who has already had the worst day of his life and is glad of company. "There's fifty-two minutes gone off my slate. My own snips did it. And I went down the Stair and stood at that door and I don't know what I came for."

"Hell of a thing to carry up," Dey said. "Lighter than a crate, though."

"Shut up, Dey."

"Asking for help twice in one night. It's a new me."

Nia had the paper log open on her knee under the deck light, pencil behind her ear, and she didn't look up. "Thirty-one meters," she said. "You keyed the deck and said, *I went for the can.* Then the wire scrambled you and you said it again. Same words, same voice. Like you were checking your own work." She turned the pencil around and wrote it in the column under the boat rule — slates run, nobody cuts, nobody goes down alone — small and square, the way somebody writes when paper is the only thing on board that nobody has edited.

"That," Nia said. "You went for that." She held the log out so Wren could see her own sentence in Nia's handwriting. "Now it's on the page. It isn't yours to lose anymore."

Bayo crouched at the drum with one palm flat on the housing, which was doing nothing for anybody. "You did good," he said warmly. "You both did real good. That rig's on the water, it's minutes—"

"It's committed to a barge out east with its lights off," Nia said.

"Then I'll hold the rail." He put both hands on the rail.

Wren got her elbow under herself. The beacon ticked on in her fist, patient, one a second, aimed at nobody. Sol was looking at her with her jaw set and rain running off her chin, and Wren could see the exact place where the captain reached for something she already knew and found the shelf bare, and covered it over.

"Deck clock says four," Sol said.

Then Salas sat back on his heels. He spat, wiped his mouth with the back of his wrist, and what the deep had left of his voice came up from somewhere under the floor of him.

"Open it, girl," he said. "You went down and you paid for it. Let's see what you bought."

Wren got the can out of her hand with the help of her other hand. The fingers had set like a hook, and the clasp took a chip of skin with it, and the beacon went on chirping against her palm the whole time, one a second, patient as a drip in a bilge.

"Under the beam," Sol said. "Not out here."

The sealed beam was eight feet of salvaged shop window lashed over the aft deck on four stanchions, the only dry square on the boat, and under it the rain turned into a noise in the roof instead of a thing hitting you. Nia dragged the mat sideways. Salas got himself up on one knee and stayed there, breathing like a man who'd been sick and was annoyed about it.

Bayo came with the field head in both arms, the way you carry something at a christening. It was a hand reader: a thumb-crank generator on the left, a reading head on the right, and a take-up spool between them, and it dragged a diver's wire past the head so a person could be heard dry on deck with no slate and no screen and nothing to argue with.

"Battery's good for one pass," Bayo said. "After that it's a rock."

"Crank runs the head," Wren said. "Battery's only the take-up."

She sat with her legs straight out in front of her because that was as far as they went. Her hands were stupid with cold. It took her three tries to get the wire through the guide, and then she ran it over the tension arm and onto the take-up, and the wire was thinner than a hair and steel and held an hour and fifty minutes of her life.

Four fingers from the end, her thumb found the join. A snip and a splice, laid neat, the ends twisted and tinned by somebody who did this for a living and had done it in the dark.

"You could skip it," Dey said from the mat. The bag went in and out in Sol's other hand. "Crank it, let it tell us whatever you like. Cheaper."

"You want the truth or the lung rig?"

"Both. I'm indentured, not fussy."

She took the shears out of her chest pocket. Reader's shears, short, blunt-nosed, one blade notched for wire, the notch worn bright from twenty years of her own thumb. There was a way to do this that took six minutes. Snip the span, twist the ends, hand up a can with a hole in it. The record would say a diver went down for the can and came back with the can, and nobody on this deck would ever hear what she'd said through four inches of steel door, and she would be the only person alive who knew she'd said it.

Out past the beam the dark hull sat against the rail with nothing lit on it at all, close enough that she could hear water slapping a fender, and nobody aboard had a lamp to spare to look at it. Quill's channel was still open on the deck speaker, quiet, a woman with a book on her knee and a bell to beat.

"Wire only tells once," Wren said. "Whatever the head reads, it takes with it."

"Then read it slow," Salas said. He had his lamp off. Water was still coming out of him in a thin thread onto the deck.

"Wren." Sol said it the way she said things to a green diver at the rail, and then she said the rest of it flat, out loud, for the whole boat. "Slates run. Nobody cuts. Nobody goes down alone."

She didn't reach for the shears. That was the worst part. She stood there with the rain running off her chin and her jaw set, and she waited.

Bayo put both hands back on the rail and held it.

Overhead the deck clock turned over to three. The beacon ticked in Wren's fist, aimed at nobody, and she put her thumb in the notch of the shears and opened them over the wire.

She closed the shears. The notch let go of the wire with a small tick, metal off metal, and she slid them back into the chest pocket and did the flap up, because her hands wanted a job and that was the only one she had for them.

"There," she said.

Sol didn't nod. From Sol that was a parade.

Wren set her thumb on the crank. The field head was older than she was, the handle worn pale and smooth where a hundred divers had ground out their last bad minutes on decks like this one, and it wanted to be turned slow. Slow and the head read clean. Fast and the wire chattered and you lost the soft parts, the parts where a voice broke.

She turned it slow.

The take-up spool took up the slack with a tick. Behind the head the wire went blank as it passed, the way it always did, the reading and the eating the same motion. For a second there was nothing but rain on the beam overhead and the beacon in her fist, patient, one a second, and Dey's bag going in and out, and then the head found the groove and the first sound came up out of the little paper cone Bayo held.

It was a throat clearing. Wet, unhurried, the scrape of somebody settling in to speak with no hurry about it at all. It filled the dry square under the beam, and it was the same sound, the exact same sound, that had come down the comms pair at thirty-one meters while she hung on the line with no one on the surface end to make it.

Bayo's face did the thing. The small one, a pull at one corner of the mouth, there and gone, like a man who's heard his own name said in a room he'd been sure was empty. He took his hand off the rail and put it back.

"That's not you," Sol said.

"No," Wren said.

"Whose is it?"

"I don't know. I've heard it once before." She kept the handle moving. "Tonight."

Then her own voice came out of the cone.

There was no mistaking it. The pitch of it, the way it sat a little high, and under that the small upward lift she put on the end of a sentence when she wanted a person to feel minded after. She hadn't known she did that. Hearing it from the outside she didn't care for it. It was the voice she kept for frightened people, and she was using it now, through four inches of steel door, on a man she had gone up the stair and left in the dark.

"—alright, Ivo," the voice said, warm as bathwater. "Alright. Listen to me now."

On his knee Salas went still. Lamp off, face turned to the little cone, he listened the way a man listens to his own name read out of a will.

"You're gonna be fine," said the voice that was hers and was fourteen months and forty-two meters old. "I've got you. Keep the light off, keep breathing slow, and I'm gonna—"

The crank turned. The beacon ticked. Behind the head the wire went white and empty.

"I'm gonna get you out," her voice said, and the lift climbed higher on it, coaxing, kind, a lie already halfway out of its own mouth. "Help's already coming, Ivo. You hear me? Help is already—"

"—coming. The drum's already turning, Ivo. You hear that? That's the drum. Hold on for me. Just hold on."

The cone clicked and gave up nothing after it but the take-up spool ticking over slack, the crank still going slow under Wren's thumb, and rain on the beam overhead.

Nobody said anything for a while. Dey's bag went in and out. Out past the beam the dark hull took water against its fender, unhurried, like it had all night and knew it.

"There's no drum on that," Salas said.

He was still on his knee with his lamp off and he said it the way a man reads a gauge.

"No," Wren said. "There isn't."

"Forty-two meters and a steel door and no drum." He wiped his mouth with the back of his wrist. "I'd have heard a drum. I heard everything else down there for fourteen months. I heard the tide turn."

"I didn't key a channel. I didn't log a call. I went up the stair with the drum still lashed and the wire slack and I told a man behind a door that help was on the way." She kept the handle moving. "I told myself somebody else had the watch."

"Somebody did," Nia said, not looking up.

"Not that night."

Salas was quiet a moment. "I'd have waited longer."

"I know."

"That's not a comfort, girl, that's arithmetic. Fourteen months is nothing much. I'd have waited till the tower came down on me." He got his other knee under himself and stayed there. "What I wouldn't have done is thank you. Warm's the worst thing you can hand a man in the dark. Warm makes him hold on. So don't hand me any more of it."

"Understood."

"Say it like you mean it or don't say it."

"I'll not be warm to you again," Wren said, flat and level, no lift on the end of it at all.

"Better," Salas said.

Dey laughed from the mat and the laugh turned into the other thing halfway through, and Sol tipped the bag for him until he had it back.

"Fourteen months," he said, when he could. "Not one call. Not a whistle. And I'm the one in the book as won't ask for help." He rolled his head toward her. "I asked twice tonight. Twice. I'm practically a town crier."

"You're practically a lung case."

"Both can be true."

"Nobody could've—" Bayo started, warm, from the drum.

"You could've," Nia said.

Bayo put both hands back on the rail and held it.

Nia turned the pencil around. "Do I write the words?"

"Not yet."

"Then I'm writing that they were played." She wrote it small and square and drew a line under it. "Eleven seconds, deck heard it. That's all a log's for."

The deck clock still said three. It had said three for a long time now, which was the worst way for a clock to behave.

Wren's right hand stayed on the crank, because that was the job. Her left came off her knee by itself, the can shut in it with the beacon going, one a second, patient, aimed at nobody, and crossed her body to the chest pocket. Two fingers found the flap. Her thumb went through the cloth and settled into the notch of the shears the way it had been cut there over twenty years.

There was nothing left to cut. Everything past her thumb was already read and going blank behind the head. Her hand didn't care. It knew one motion.

On the open channel a chair creaked, and Quill's voice came up out of the deck speaker small and even, a woman with a book on her knee and a bell to beat, saying that she had heard the wire, and that she was obliged to say so, and the hull out in the dark came against the rail hard enough to move the whole boat a hand's width sideways.

The crank went round twice more on nothing. The take-up spool ticked over slack, and then the tail of the wire came up out of the tension arm and flicked the back of Wren's hand, the way a line does when the fly's gone and you didn't feel it go.

She lifted the spool off the post and turned it to the deck light. Blank end to end, dull as spent fuse wire, an hour and fifty minutes of her life gone gray.

"Again," Dey said.

"Can't. The head eats what it reads. There's no groove left in it to find." She set the spool down. "That's it. It's in nine heads on this deck now, and out of the deck speaker onto an open channel, so it's in the Kettle's ear as well. Nobody can go back and check me on it. Nobody can check *you* on it either, Ivo. You heard it once and you'll hear it your own way for the rest of your life."

"I heard it," Salas said. "Say it dry. Out of your mouth, no lift on the end."

Wren turned on her hip to face him. Her hands were shaking, so she put them flat on the deck.

"Ivo. I called nobody. There's no drum turning and no boat on the way and I'm going up. I've got a little air left and I'm spending it on the ladder. Keep your lamp off, it only shows you the door." She took a breath. "And I told myself somebody else had the watch."

"Say that last part again."

"Somebody else had the watch."

"Better." He didn't look at her. "Now we're both carrying something."

Nia wrote it. She wrote small and square, in the column under the boat rule, and it took her longer than eleven seconds because she got the commas right, and then she read it back the way she'd read it into a court.

"*Eleven seconds, wire played, deck heard: Ivo, I called nobody.*" She drew a line under it. "Now it's on the page. It isn't yours to lose."

The clock over the wheelhouse still said three.

"Then where'd the other fifty-two go?" Wren said. "Last night. Somebody put me down that tower and brought me back and cut it out of my own wire, and I want to know who's got the piece they took."

Nobody answered right away. Rain in the roof of the beam. Dey's bag going in and out.

"I've got the hour you gave me back," Sol said. "That's the whole shelf. Before that it's bare."

"I was on the dock with the orange knots," Bayo said, warm. "All night, I was—"

"You were," Nia said, and let it sit there.

"I was gray on this mat," Dey said. "Ask anybody. I'm a witness to my own bad night."

Nia turned the paper back, page over page, and held it up. "Horn order. Deck light. Bell at ten. Nothing about a line off this boat, because nobody wrote it down. Paper only knows what somebody puts on it."

"I don't have last night," Salas said. "I don't have tonight much either. Don't ask me for it."

Wren looked at the can in her left hand, ticking, one a second, patient, and the battery gauge in the end cap showed a little under half. Six hours of chirp on a box with nothing left on it, calling a boat that was already sitting on top of it, and the crew all breathing and none of them coming.

"Somebody had the watch," she said.

Out past the beam the hull against the rail took the Marrow's weight and settled, and nobody aboard had a lamp to spare to see who was standing on it.
